# Overview {-}

**Author:** Sean Westwood

Part of the [demystR](https://demystr.github.io) series.

The drift diffusion model (DDM) is one of the most widely used models of how people make
two-choice decisions. It explains two things at once: which option someone chooses, and
how long they take to choose it. It is usually fitted with a package, and the package
becomes a black box: data go in, parameters come out.

This book builds the model from scratch instead. Every part of it is shown three ways:

- **the equation**: what the model says, in mathematical notation;
- **the code**: the same thing written in R, usually one line per term of the equation;
- **the picture**: a figure showing what that code does.

<div class="summary-box">
If you can point at a term in an equation, find the line of code that computes it, and
see what it does in a figure, you understand that part of the model. The book is built
so that you can do that for every part of the DDM.
</div>

By the end of Part 1 you will have written:

- a simulator that produces decisions one small step at a time;
- the formula for the probability of each response at each response time;
- a function that fits the model to data by maximum likelihood;
- checks that the fitted model describes the data, and that the fitting recovers known values.

## Who This Book Is For {-}

You should be comfortable with basic R, including the tidyverse (`dplyr` pipelines and
`ggplot2`), and with the idea of a probability distribution. The model itself is written
in plain R, one line per term of each equation, so you can see every calculation. You do not need to know any calculus: the
book introduces the little it uses from the beginning, and an appendix goes further for
anyone who wants to.

## How The Book Is Organised {-}

**Part 1: Perceptual Decisions.** The model is built and fitted using a random-dot
motion task, where people decide whether a cloud of dots is moving left or right. This
is the task the DDM is most often taught with, and each of its parameters matches
something about the task that is easy to picture.

**Part 2: Value-Based Decisions.** The same model is applied to choices between options
of different value, where the drift depends on how much better one option is than the
other.

**Later chapters** add models fitted to a whole group at once (hierarchical models).

The chapters shown in grey italics in the contents have not been written yet; each one describes
what it will cover.

## The Data {-}

The data in Part 1 are simulated, with known true parameter values, so you can always
check whether a fit recovered what was put in. The script that made them is
`data-raw/simulate_rdm.R` in the book's repository.
